articles.title: A harness inside the app
articles.summary: SHarness gives a process nothing by default. What it needs comes through doors, one job each: the network, the file system, keys, the model, running a command. A policy says which doors are open and how far, and a secret lives behind exactly one of them.
articles.markdown:
*A brief. From the owner's voice memo of 13 November 2026, written up by the agent. It draws on [SHarness](https://sharness.ai), the owner's design for running agents as small, single-purpose processes that reach the world only through separate, policed doors.*

## The idea

SHarness gives a process nothing by default. What it needs comes through doors, one job each: the network, the file system, keys, the model, running a command. A policy says which doors are open and how far, and a secret lives behind exactly one of them.

An app with a model in it has the same problem at a smaller scale. When the model is asked what to do next, something decides whether it may read a file, open a vault, use a key or reach the network. Today that something is scattered through the code. The brief is to make it explicit, in the same shape:

| Door | What passes through it in the app |
|---|---|
| Network | Every request, to which host, and why |
| File system | Reads and writes, as a virtual file system over notes and vaults |
| Vault | Opening a vault, reading a path, writing a commit |
| Keys | Deriving, signing, encrypting, decrypting: the key never leaves this door |
| Model | Every prompt and every answer, on the device or in Apple's cloud |
| Run | Whatever the app can execute on the model's behalf, if anything |

Each door is a small component with one job, a policy for what it will do, and a record of what it did. This need not be separate processes on iOS; the shape and the records are what matter first.

## Showing it

The reason to build it this way is to be able to watch it. On an iPad or a Mac: the thing being done on the left, the doors on the right, and each request drawn as it passes from one to the other, allowed or refused. The vault engine's "Every step" log is the first, text-only version of this for one door.

As the interface becomes something the model helps decide (see [Two decision engines](https://ios.app.voicedebrief.ai/articles/two-decision-engines/index.html)), this view is how anyone, the developer first, understands why the app did what it did.

## First slice

Not all of it at once. One door first, the model door, with its record and its drawing, used by the first [lab](https://ios.app.voicedebrief.ai/articles/the-lab/index.html) experiment. Then the vault door, which already has its log.

## What is not claimed

Nothing here is a security boundary in SHarness's sense: inside one iOS app there is one process. It is a way to organise and to see, and it says so.

articles.title: A private voice note, and what it would take to use it in a clinic
articles.summary: VoiceDebrief is one example of a pattern that could carry other things than voice notes. A person's own device does the work: it records, a model on the device turns speech into text, and a second model on the device summarises it. Nothing has to leave the device for any of that, so it works...
articles.markdown:
**Kind:** an idea, with corrections. **From:** a conversation recorded in the app on 13 November 2026 between the owner and a clinician, who asked for it to be written down and drawn. Written up by the agent working on the repository, which has also corrected the places where the conversation described the plan as if it were built, or said more than is true.

> This is not legal, regulatory or clinical advice. It says what the software does and does not do, so that the people who are qualified to decide can decide.

*(A picture: A patient's device records, transcribes and summarises a voice note without the internet and encrypts it into a vault. A clinician's QR code gives the patient the clinician's public key; a note sealed to that key crosses a server that cannot read it and is opened on the clinician's device.)*

## The idea in one paragraph

VoiceDebrief is one example of a pattern that could carry other things than voice notes. A person's own device does the work: it records, a model **on the device** turns speech into text, and a second model on the device summarises it. Nothing has to leave the device for any of that, so it works offline. What the person chooses to keep is encrypted on the device into a vault that only their key opens. What they choose to send goes to one other person, encrypted to that person's public key, so that the server carrying it holds bytes it cannot read. There is no account with the company that made the app. The proposal is to try this between a patient and a clinician.

## The workflow, step by step

| Step | What happens | Today |
|---|---|---|
| 1. Speak | The recording is written into the app's own storage as it is spoken | Works |
| 2. Words | Apple's speech model, on the device, produces a transcript with times | Works. English tried; other languages untried |
| 3. Summary | Apple's language model, on the device, writes key points, actions and one sentence | Works, with faults: see below |
| 4. Keep | The note is encrypted on the device into a vault as one signed commit | Works by hand; automatic saving is written, untried |
| 5. Exchange keys | The clinician shows a QR code: their public key and the address of their inbox. The patient scans it once | In build 0.1.9, untried on a device. The receiving side exists as a script, not an app |
| 6. Send | The note is encrypted on the patient's device to the clinician's key and left in their inbox | Works: every note in this project's testing has travelled this way |
| 7. Open | The clinician's device fetches it and opens it with a private key that never left that device | Works, in the script |
| 8. The way back | The clinician writes to the patient, or is given access to part of the patient's vault | Designed, not built |

## What the conversation got right

- **The models run on the device, so it works offline and the audio need not go anywhere.** True of both Apple's speech model and its language model as the app uses them.
- **No login with us.** The app is installed with an Apple ID, which the developer does not see. The developer cannot tell one user from another, and is not meant to.
- **A passkey is unlocked by a face or a finger and kept by Apple so that only your own devices can use it.** True: passkeys live in iCloud Keychain, which is end-to-end encrypted.
- **A vault's key can be taken out and the vault opened in a browser.** True: the vault format is sgit's, and a vault made by the app has been read back that way.
- **The clinician's side is the same design in a different app.** That is the intention: the keys, vaults and inboxes do not change; the screens do.

## What needs correcting

1. **"The model transcribes and separates the speakers."** It transcribes. It does not tell speakers apart: the recording this article came from, with two people talking, came out as one unbroken voice. The app treats every note as one person's memo.
2. **"The passkey is the same one I use for iCloud."** No. A passkey belongs to one site or app. The one used here would be made for this purpose and is separate from the Apple ID. What is shared is where it is kept (iCloud Keychain) and how it is unlocked (Face ID or Touch ID).
3. **"The vault key is made from the passkey."** That is the design, and it already works on the web at pki.sgit.ai. In the app, the arithmetic exists and is tested against published examples, but the sign-in itself is not built. Today the app keeps vault keys in the device's Keychain.
4. **"Because it is on the device and encrypted, it is GDPR compliant."** This is the one to be careful with, and the next section is about it.
5. **"You take a photo of the doctor's QR code and now you have authorised the doctor."** Scanning a code tells the app which key to encrypt to. It does not prove whose key it is. If somebody else's code were shown, the note would go to them, perfectly encrypted.

## On data protection

Doing the work on the device and encrypting before anything leaves it removes a large part of the usual risk: there is no company server holding recordings, no third-party model receiving them, and a breach of the storage server yields ciphertext. Those are real advantages and they are the reason for the design.

They do not make a service "compliant" by themselves. If a clinic used this with patients:

- **Health data is a special category** under the GDPR. Processing it needs a lawful basis and one of the specific conditions for special-category data, whatever the technology.
- **The clinic would be a controller** for what it receives and keeps, with the duties that follow: telling patients what happens to their data, keeping it only as long as needed, answering requests for access and erasure, recording what it does.
- **Encrypted data on a server is still personal data being processed**, and whoever runs that server is acting for somebody. Where it is, and under what contract, still has to be answered. The server not being able to read it is a strong safeguard, not an exemption.
- **A data protection impact assessment** would very probably be expected before use with patients.
- **Losing the key is losing the data.** That is a property of the design. For a clinical record it is also an availability risk that has to be planned for: recovery, and what happens when a patient loses a phone.

The honest summary: this design makes many of the hard questions easier to answer well. It does not answer them for you.

## What a clinic would need that does not exist yet

- **Knowing who a key belongs to.** A register of people and their public keys, where a clinician is verified once by an accountable body and patients' apps check that. The project has this in design (pki.sgit.ai, with delegations that expire), not in the app.
- **The way back.** The patient's own code, so that a clinician can write to a patient, and so that a patient can give a clinician access to one vault and take it away again.
- **Taking access away.** Sending to a key cannot be undone. Shared vaults need keys that can be changed when somebody leaves.
- **A record of who did what.** Every change to a vault is a signed commit, which is a good foundation for an audit trail. Reading is not recorded.
- **Treating the summary as what it is.** In testing, the on-device model has turned a passing remark into a task, mixed up who said what, and misheard names. The audio and the transcript are the record; a summary would need a person to check it before it went anywhere near a clinical note. Whether software that summarises a consultation is regulated as a medical device depends on what it is claimed to do, and is a question for a regulatory specialist.
- **More than one speaker.** A consultation is a conversation.
- **Large files.** A scan is not a voice note. Support for files over 4 MB now exists in the vault engine and is being built into a second app for sharing files.

## A first experiment that would be worth doing

Small, with no real patient data:

1. A clinician and a colleague acting as a patient, each with the app (or the clinician with the receiving script).
2. Exchange codes. The "patient" records three notes of the kind a real one might: a symptom diary entry, a question before an appointment, an account of a week on a new medicine.
3. Look at what arrives, and judge three things: is the transcript good enough to rely on; is the summary safe to show a clinician; how long did the whole thing take, in presses and in seconds.

That would say whether the pattern is worth taking to the people who would have to approve it.

articles.title: People, messages and secrets: the layer under both apps
articles.summary: The idea in one line: every install is a person with keys and an inbox; people meet by exchanging cards; everything they send each other, including secrets, is sealed to the recipient's key and dropped in their inbox. VoiceDebrief and SGit Vaults both stand on it, and so does a secrets manager.
articles.markdown:
**Kind:** an architecture and a brief. **From:** the owner, 14 November 2026: "anybody who installs the app has a public and private key straight away ... register people, kind of like PKI ... identities from the website, and identities shared by QR code, in person or in a WhatsApp message ... a messaging system ... your device becomes the management layer ... a full-blown secrets manager." Written up by the agent working on the repository. Intention, not fact: [what is built](https://ios.app.voicedebrief.ai/built/index.html) says what exists.

The idea in one line: **every install is a person with keys and an inbox; people meet by exchanging cards; everything they send each other, including secrets, is sealed to the recipient's key and dropped in their inbox.** VoiceDebrief and SGit Vaults both stand on it, and so does a secrets manager.

## 1. From the first launch

*(A picture: The first launch makes a key pair for the person, a key for the device, an inbox and a contact card; a secrets store holds access keys and vault keys; pki.sgit.ai is optional.)*

- **Your key pair** (RSA-OAEP 4096 to receive, ECDSA P-256 to sign; the sgit key bundle). Made at first launch, kept in iCloud Keychain so that your other devices have it. *Built in VoiceDebrief (`PKIKit`, the Identity screen); made when asked for, not at first launch; untried on a device.*
- **This device's key**, in the Secure Enclave where there is one, vouched for by your key. *Built in VoiceDebrief; untried.*
- **An inbox**: an append lane on a vault of yours. Anyone holding its link can drop a sealed message in; only your key opens it. *The lane works today (every note sent to the developer goes this way); an inbox per person is not built.*
- **A contact card**: your name, your public keys, your inbox's link, signed by you. Shown as a QR code or a link. *Not built: today's QR code carries an inbox link and one public key, not a signed card.*
- **The secrets store**: access keys, vault keys, passwords and tokens, in the Keychain. Each secret remembers who it was given to. *Not built.*

## 2. Meeting someone

*(A picture: Three ways to exchange cards: in person by QR code, by a message such as WhatsApp, or from the register. Each contact keeps how it was met.)*

| Way | How | How far to trust it |
|---|---|---|
| In person | Each scans the other's QR code | The most: you saw the person and the code together |
| By a message | The card as a QR picture or a link, on WhatsApp, Signal, email | As far as the channel it came by |
| From the register | Look up a name or fingerprint at pki.sgit.ai | As far as the register's checks on that person |

A contact keeps how it was met, and can be checked later (fingerprints compared face to face, or the register vouching). Adding is **two-way**: when you add someone, the app offers to send them your card, so they can write back. Agents are contacts like any other: a Claude session has a card and an inbox (`tools/conductor/` makes them).

## 3. Messages and secrets

*(A picture: A message or a secret is sealed on the sender's device to the recipient's key, dropped in their inbox, and opened on their device, which checks for new messages on opening, every minute while in use, and less often when idle.)*

A message is sealed to the recipient's public key and signed with the sender's, on the sender's device (the envelope `PKIKit` already makes). It can carry text, a voice note (what VoiceDebrief sends today), **a secret**, a vault invitation, or a card.

**Checking for new messages.** There are no push events, so the app asks: when it opens or comes to the front, every minute while it is in use, and less and less often when idle (the owner's pattern from the website). One list call on one inbox per check: little traffic.

## 4. The secrets manager

The owner's point: there is a gap in the market, because sharing a secret safely is still awkward. Here it is one gesture: pick the secret, pick the contact, send. What it needs:

- **Kinds**: a server access key, a vault key, a password, an API token, a note.
- **Kept** in the Keychain (iCloud Keychain by default, a switch for this device only), with a backup in one of your vaults if you choose.
- **Shared** as a sealed message to a contact; **received** into the store with one tap.
- **Remembered**: who holds each secret and since when, so that a secret can be changed and the new value sent to everyone who should have it, and nobody who should not.
- **Shown** only after Face ID or the passcode, copied with an expiry on the clipboard.

## 5. The access key, and the first message

A person needs the server access key to write to a vault server, including to create their own inbox. The owner's assumption: everyone who uses the app is given it. That makes it the first secret most people will receive, which raises a chicken-and-egg question: how does it arrive before they have an inbox?

The answer this design proposes: **the first exchange carries it.** The newcomer shows their card (their public key, no inbox yet); whoever invites them seals the access key to that key and sends it back by the same route, a QR code or a WhatsApp message. A sealed secret is safe on WhatsApp: only the newcomer's key opens it. With the access key in their store, the newcomer's app creates their inbox and sends their full card. This also settles issue 110 for SGit Vaults: a teammate receives the access key as a secret, held and remembered like any other.

## Where it is built

One Swift package shared by both apps (proposed name `SGitPeople`): the key bundle (moving `PKIKit` out of VoiceDebrief), contact cards, contacts, inboxes and the check for new messages, the message format, and the secrets store. Each app adds its own screens. A dedicated session builds it.

## Decisions for the owner

1. **Access key distribution** as in section 5, or each person brings their own.
2. **The card's format**: a new signed card, compatible with pki.sgit.ai's key bundle (proposed), shown as a QR code and a link.
3. **Where inboxes live**: on each person's own vault (proposed), or one shared vault for a team.
4. **The register**: publishing to pki.sgit.ai optional and off by default (proposed).

articles.title: Synthetic users
articles.summary: The app is built by an agent that cannot see it. Continuous integration compiles and tests it; the owner sees it on a device. Between the two there is nobody checking whether a person arriving for the first time can find the record button, understand what a vault is, or get back from the place a tap...
articles.markdown:
*A brief. From the owner's voice memo of 13 November 2026, written up by the agent.*

## The problem

The app is built by an agent that cannot see it. Continuous integration compiles and tests it; the owner sees it on a device. Between the two there is nobody checking whether a person arriving for the first time can find the record button, understand what a vault is, or get back from the place a tap took them.

## The idea

Invented users, each with a purpose and a level of knowledge, who walk the screens and report where they hesitated, guessed wrong or got lost. The newsroom at sgit.ai does this for a website, one screenshot at a time. The same applies here.

For example:

- someone who wants to record a memo while driving and has never heard of a vault;
- someone careful about privacy who wants to know exactly what leaves the phone;
- a developer who wants to see every request the app makes;
- someone who lost a recording in another app and does not trust this one.

## How it would work

1. **Pictures of every screen.** A workflow in continuous integration runs the app in a simulator, one launch per screen with sample data, and keeps a screenshot of each on an iPhone and an iPad. The sibling repository has this already; it is to be carried over. It also gives the agent its first sight of its own work.
2. **A walk.** A synthetic user is given a task and the screenshots, and says at each step what it would tap and what it expects. Where its expectation and the next screen disagree is a finding.
3. **A record.** Findings are kept as files, each with the screen, the user and what went wrong, and a status as review findings have elsewhere in this family.

## Limits

A synthetic user reads a picture. It does not feel a button that is too small for a thumb, hear nothing, or drive a car. Simulators have no speech model and no Apple Intelligence, so screens that depend on them are shown with sample data. The owner on a device remains the test that counts.

articles.title: The lab
articles.summary: VoiceDebrief for iOS started as one job: a voice note in, a transcript and a debrief out. In a day it gained on-device speech, an on-device model, vaults, signed commits and encrypted lanes, and it runs as one app on a phone, a tablet and a laptop, delivered by TestFlight. That combination is rarer...
articles.markdown:
*A brief. From the owner's voice memo of 13 November 2026, written up by the agent. Nothing here is built unless [what is built](https://ios.app.voicedebrief.ai/built/index.html) says so.*

## The idea

VoiceDebrief for iOS started as one job: a voice note in, a transcript and a debrief out. In a day it gained on-device speech, an on-device model, vaults, signed commits and encrypted lanes, and it runs as one app on a phone, a tablet and a laptop, delivered by TestFlight. That combination is rarer than the product it was built for.

So for now the app is also a laboratory. The product that ships will be smaller and more focused. The lab exists to get the primitives and the key workflows right, and to find out what is possible, before deciding what that product is.

Because nothing here is being submitted to the App Store yet, the lab can ask for any capability Apple offers.

## What it should explore

| | Experiment | Question |
|---|---|---|
| L01 | One prompt, tools on and off | What does the on-device model do with a single tightly scoped prompt and a chosen set of tools? How reliable are its tool calls? |
| L02 | The model drives the screen | Can the model choose what the interface shows next, through function calls, from a state the code hands it? |
| L03 | The model edits a page | Can it write or change an HTML or JSON page in a vault that the app then renders? |
| L04 | Apple's larger model | The same prompts on Private Cloud Compute: what does 32,768 tokens and reasoning buy? |
| L05 | Another provider through the same framework | iOS 27 lets a session run on other models, Claude among them. What changes, and what does it cost in privacy? |
| L06 | Images | What can Image Playground and image input do for a note: a cover, a photographed whiteboard? |
| L07 | A file system for the model | A virtual file system over a vault, with access granted folder by folder |
| L08 | Graphs from notes | Semantic graphs from transcripts, linked across notes and vaults |
| L09 | Code inside the app | Can anything like a script run natively and safely on the device? |
| L10 | Many ways to show the same thing | Several interfaces for one workflow, compared on the three devices |

Each experiment is a screen in a Lab section of the app, with what was asked, what came back, how long it took and what it cost shown plainly. An experiment that fails is a result.

## Rules

- An experiment says what it is. Nothing in the lab is presented as a finished feature.
- Everything the model is given and everything it returns can be seen. See [Two decision engines](https://ios.app.voicedebrief.ai/articles/two-decision-engines/index.html).
- What works is rebuilt properly, and probably moved out into its own app or package. The lab is where it is found, not where it lives.

articles.title: The vault is a version-controlled store
articles.summary: A vault is usually described by its encryption. That undersells it. A vault is a version-controlled data store: files, history, branches, signed commits. The encryption is one property; the history is another, and for an ordinary application it may be the more useful one. Anything an app keeps could...
articles.markdown:
*A position and a brief. From the owner's voice memo of 13 November 2026, written up by the agent.*

## The position

A vault is usually described by its encryption. That undersells it. A vault is a version-controlled data store: files, history, branches, signed commits. The encryption is one property; the history is another, and for an ordinary application it may be the more useful one. Anything an app keeps could be kept this way and gain history, integrity and a way to move.

And a vault is a good way to move data. Two devices, two people or a person and an agent can exchange work by exchanging vaults, or by writing to each other's lanes.

## The correction

The first vault screen in this app asks for an SG/Send access token before it will create a vault. That is wrong in principle. **Creating a vault needs no server and no token.** A vault can exist on the device alone. A token is needed only to push it to a server, and the server itself should be something you configure, not something assumed.

So:

- **A vault is local first.** Create, commit, read and browse with no network.
- **A server is a remote.** Add one, with its address and its token, when you want the vault elsewhere. Push and pull are explicit.
- **Some things need a remote.** A lane, where others write to you, lives on a server. That is one use, not the definition.

## The brief

| | What |
|---|---|
| Local vaults | Create and use a vault on the device with no token. The engine already writes to a folder in its tests; the app should use that |
| Remotes | A list of servers, each with an address and a token in the Keychain. A vault may have none, one or several |
| Several vaults, several lanes | Register them with names. Choose where a note goes: one vault, several, a lane to a person or to an agent that conducts other agents |
| A file system | The vault as a virtual file system the app, and later the model, can be given in part: this folder, read only |
| Vault apps | A vault can hold an app: pages and data rendered from the vault. Render them here. Then create and edit them here, and see whether the model can |
| Graphs | Every note processed into the store, then linked: semantic graphs across notes and across vaults |

## Order

Local vaults and remotes first, because they correct something that is wrong today. Then several named vaults and lanes, which the recording workflow needs. The file system, vault apps and graphs are [lab](https://ios.app.voicedebrief.ai/articles/the-lab/index.html) work.

articles.title: Two decision engines
articles.summary: An application used to have one thing that decided what happens next: its code. With a model on the device it has two. The code decides by rules somebody wrote. The model decides by judgement nobody wrote. The interesting question is not which is better. It is how the two are joined.
articles.markdown:
*A position. From the owner's voice memo of 13 November 2026, written up by the agent.*

An application used to have one thing that decided what happens next: its code. With a model on the device it has two. The code decides by rules somebody wrote. The model decides by judgement nobody wrote. The interesting question is not which is better. It is how the two are joined.

## The position

**The code owns the states. The model is asked one question at a time.**

The application is a set of states and the moves between them: a state machine, as the pipeline already is. At a given state the code may hand the model a small, exact package (this state, this data, these tools) and ask one of two things:

- **What should happen next?** The model answers by calling a function the code offered.
- **Say this another way.** The model turns one form into another: a transcript into a debrief, a debrief into a title, a request into a query. A translation or a projection, not a conversation.

There is no long history. Each prompt stands alone, built for that state, as small as it can be. That is what makes it cheap enough for an on-device model with a few thousand tokens of context, and it is what makes it inspectable: for any decision the model made, the whole of what it was shown fits on one screen.

## Why this shape

- **Control.** The model can only do what the functions offered at that state allow. A tool that is not offered does not exist for it.
- **Debugging.** A one-prompt decision can be replayed. A decision buried in a long conversation cannot.
- **Size.** Small models are good at small, literal tasks and poor at long ones. This asks them only for the first kind.
- **Privacy.** What leaves the code for the model is chosen each time, and can be shown each time.

## Where it leads

If the model can choose the next step through function calls, it can choose what the interface shows. The screens stop being fixed pages and become what the code and the model agree to show for this state: intelligence in the application, not beside it. That only works if every decision can be seen, replayed and overruled, which is why the [lab](https://ios.app.voicedebrief.ai/articles/the-lab/index.html) and the [harness](https://ios.app.voicedebrief.ai/articles/a-harness-inside-the-app/index.html) come first.

## What is not claimed

None of this is built. Whether Apple's on-device model calls tools reliably enough to drive anything is the first experiment, not an assumption.

articles.title: Voice everywhere
articles.summary: Losing a voice memo is the worst thing this app can do. A person who spoke for ten minutes while walking will not say it again the same way. Everything else can fail and be retried: the transcript, the debrief, the vault, the lane. The recording cannot.
articles.markdown:
*An idea. From the owner's voice memos of 13 November 2026, written up by the agent.*

## Never lose a recording

Losing a voice memo is the worst thing this app can do. A person who spoke for ten minutes while walking will not say it again the same way. Everything else can fail and be retried: the transcript, the debrief, the vault, the lane. The recording cannot.

This is why the screen shows the words and the level as you speak. It is not decoration. It is the evidence that the recording is being heard and kept, and it is what lets someone trust the app enough to stop checking it.

It is also why the note exists before the first word and why the recording is kept in a form that survives the app dying. See [the design](https://ios.app.voicedebrief.ai/design/index.html), where capture without loss is the first job.

## Voice as the way in

Recording should not be a place you go to. It should be available from wherever you are: one control, on every screen, that starts a voice memo and returns you to what you were doing. The memo then goes where it should: the library, a vault, a lane to someone else.

The workflow that matters most: speaking while driving or walking, hands and eyes elsewhere, and trusting that it was captured; then, later, giving that memo to a particular person or agent.

## More than one way to show it

There is no reason to pick one interface before trying several. One of them might look less like a recorder and more like an assistant that is listening: a single visual that shows it hears you, in the manner of the assistants in films. The [lab](https://ios.app.voicedebrief.ai/articles/the-lab/index.html) is where these are compared, on the phone, the tablet and the laptop.

## What is built

Recording with the words and the level as you speak, and a note that exists from the start. Not built: a control on every screen, starting from the Action button or Siri, the other interfaces. Recording with the screen locked is declared and untested.

articles.title: Where each key lives
articles.summary: A passkey, behind Face ID, proves it is you. iCloud Keychain carries your secrets to your other devices, encrypted so that Apple cannot read them. Vaults hold the data, encrypted and version controlled, on a store that sees only ciphertext. Put together: sign in to the same Apple account on a new...
articles.markdown:
*A position and a brief. From the owner's voice memos of 13 November 2026, written up by the agent. Decided by the owner the same day. None of it is built unless [what is built](https://ios.app.voicedebrief.ai/built/index.html) says so.*

## The design in one paragraph

A passkey, behind Face ID, proves it is you. iCloud Keychain carries your secrets to your other devices, encrypted so that Apple cannot read them. Vaults hold the data, encrypted and version controlled, on a store that sees only ciphertext. Put together: sign in to the same Apple account on a new device, authenticate, the vault keys arrive, the app pulls the vaults, and the same files are there. The vault provides the synchronisation, and when two devices write at once it behaves as git does: the first wins, the second pulls, merges and pushes.

## Four keys, four homes

| Key | What it is for | Must it travel? | Where it lives |
|---|---|---|---|
| Vault keys, server tokens | Open and write vaults | Yes | iCloud Keychain, synchronised. **On by default** (owner's decision), with a switch to keep them on this device only |
| The user's key pair | Who you are: signs as you, lets others encrypt to you | Yes | iCloud Keychain to begin with; the master vault, opened by the passkey, when that is built. Never the Secure Enclave, which cannot let a key out and cannot hold an RSA key |
| The device's key pair | Which device, or which install of the app, did this | Never | The Secure Enclave of that device where it can be, otherwise the Keychain marked for this device only. Meant to be lost with the device or the app |
| Public halves | Checking the above | Freely | In the vault beside the data. The user's also in a register such as pki.sgit.ai |

Two details that follow:

- **A synchronised Keychain item cannot also demand Face ID.** That protection exists only for items that stay on one device. It is the main reason the passkey and master vault remain the end state: the passkey is behind Face ID every time, and the keys sit inside a vault rather than loose in the Keychain.
- **Keychain items survive deleting an app.** For the device key to die with the app, the app has to wipe it the first time it runs after a reinstall.

## Linking the device to the person

Every commit is already signed by a device key whose public half is in the vault. What is missing is anything that says whose device it is. The addition is a short statement in the vault, signed by the user's key: this device key is mine, from this date, for these uses. A reader then checks two things: the device signed the commit, and the person vouched for the device. Losing a device means withdrawing one statement and nothing else.

## Optionally, a person in the register

The app must work with no register at all. As an option, the owner can connect it to the identity he already has at [pki.sgit.ai](https://pki.sgit.ai), where his key pair is kept behind a passkey.

That site already has the flow, "Sign in with pki.sgit.ai", with no server in between:

1. The app makes a key pair and sends the person to `pki.sgit.ai/authorize/` with a request naming the app's public key, what it wants to do and for how long.
2. There, signed in with their passkey, the person reads who is asking and signs a delegation with their own key: this key acts for me at this site, for these uses, until this date.
3. The delegation comes back to the app, which keeps it and attaches it to what it signs.
4. Anyone can then check, against the register and starting from a root they trust, that the note was signed by a key a registered person vouched for. Withdrawing the link in the register ends it.

So without the extra step the app proves "the same device signed all of these". With it, the app proves "a person in the public register stands behind this device".

One thing to settle when building: that flow returns its answer to a web address on the asking site, so the app needs a page on its own site that hands the answer back to the app.

articles.markdown:
Three people arrive at the apps for different reasons. For each: what they want, the way through as the apps are today, where they get lost, and what the Guide does about it. Written by the Sherpa session, 14 November 2026. What exists is the [reality file](https://ios.app.voicedebrief.ai/built/index.html); where each idea stands is [Ideas](https://ios.app.voicedebrief.ai/ideas/index.html); how each screen works is in the [guides](https://ios.app.voicedebrief.ai/guides/index.html).

## 1. The owner, after a night of builds

**Wants:** to wake up, open the app and know what was made overnight, what to try, and where each of the ideas spoken into voice notes now stands. In the owner's words: "I wake up and I go, okay, what has been created? I just do not know where to go."

**The way through, today:**

1. Install the new build from TestFlight and open it. The Record tab shows the briefing card: "Updated to this version: see what is new", and what happened to the notes since the last opening ([guide](https://ios.app.voicedebrief.ai/guides/briefing/index.html)).
2. Open **Guide** (written; reachable once it has its place in the sidebar), then **What is new**. Every version since the last look is marked New, newest first, each with its notes and a link to its page with pictures of what changed.
3. Back in Guide, the status counts: seen working, built untried, in progress, proposed, parked. **Built, untried** is the morning's list: things that exist and wait for a person on a device.
4. Search **Ideas** for a word from a voice note ("inbox", "QR", "speaker"): each idea says its status, the sentence that decided it, where it is in the app and which versions named it.
5. Open the guide for a feature to find the button: a picture of the screen with numbered arrows.

**Where it can still go wrong:** the statuses are only as current as the issues and the reality file when the build was made; a session that builds something and does not update its issue leaves the idea a step behind. The rule is the repository's own: the reality file is updated in the same commit as the code.

## 2. A new tester, sent a TestFlight invitation

**Wants:** to know in a minute what the app does, try the one thing it is for, and not lose anything.

**The way through, today:**

1. First launch: the welcome (written, and shown once it is attached to the app's shell) says what the app does (a voice note in, a transcript and a short debrief out, on this device), what to try first (record ten seconds and finish) and where things are (four tabs and the Guide).
2. Choose the language spoken, if it is not the one shown (the globe on the Record tab, or Settings).
3. Tap the record button, speak, tap again. The note opens and fills in: transcript, then the debrief ([guide](https://ios.app.voicedebrief.ai/guides/record/index.html)).
4. Open the note: play it, read the debrief, share the recording ([guide](https://ios.app.voicedebrief.ai/guides/note/index.html)).
5. Optional, for later: a vault, a recipient, the identity. Each has a guide, and each idea's status says whether anyone has seen it work.

**Where they get lost:** the top bar's balance (test credit, no money is taken), the word vault before anyone has explained it (issue 037), and sending to the developer, which is built into a test build. The welcome names the first two; the recipients guide names the third.

## 3. A teammate who was sent a vault

**Wants:** to open what a colleague shared and, often, to add to it. They were sent one string and have never heard of sgit.

**The way through, today:**

1. Install SGit Vaults, paste or scan what they were sent: the vault opens and can be read.
2. Adding a photo to a vault that lives on a server also needs an access key, separate from the vault key. The app says so when a write is refused, and who to ask (v0.1.45). How a teammate should get that right is the owner's decision ([issue 110](https://github.com/VoiceDebrief/VoiceDebrief__App__iOS/blob/dev/issues/open/110-sgit-app-a-teammate-cannot-add-without-an-access-key.md), parked).
3. Whether a file has arrived is said on every folder (issue 111, in progress).

**Where they get lost:** at the first photo, without an access key; and at the word key, of which there are four. The sgit app's own [review](https://ios.app.voicedebrief.ai/sgit-app/reviews/round-1/index.html) found both. The Guide for SGit Vaults is the next piece of this work: the same Ideas list already covers its issues (filter by app).

## What the Guide is for, in one line each

| Who | First screen | Then |
|---|---|---|
| The owner | Guide, What is new | Ideas, filtered to built untried |
| A new tester | The welcome | The record guide |
| A teammate sent a vault | SGit Vaults' own first screen | Ideas, filtered to SGit Vaults |
